text: Dr. Agent: I see you're experiencing persistent vomiting and chest pain. To start, can you tell me exactly what the pain feels like and how severe it is on a scale of 1 to 10?

speaker: Patient
text: 51-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with persistent, forceful vomiting after consuming a significant amount of alcohol. His medical history includes recent treatment for Lyme disease with doxycycline. Recently, after a prolonged episode of retching, the patient starts to choke and cough forcefully, experiencing chest pain. The patient appears unable to communicate effectively at this point.

speaker: Doctor
text: The sudden onset of choking and coughing after prolonged retching is a classic sign of Boerhaave syndrome; did you experience any difficulty swallowing or a "pop" sensation in your chest right before the pain started? REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray; REQUEST IMAGES.

speaker: Measurement

The chest X-ray and images will be critical to confirm if there is a pneumomediastinum or pleural effusion. While we await those results, have you noticed any shortness of breath, fever, or a crunching sound under your skin (subcutaneous emphysema)?

REQUEST IMAGES.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Boerhaave Syndrome (Esophageal Rupture).

The clinical presentation of forceful vomiting followed by choking, severe chest pain, and the imaging findings confirm a complete rupture of the esophagus. This is a surgical emergency requiring immediate intervention.
